blocks.en: 1. The Artist’s First Painting
blocks.es_reference: 1. El primer cuadro del artista

blocks.en: Years ago a seasoned missionary in China befriended a talented young Chinese artist. Through their friendship the young artist became a Christian. He said to the missionary, “I best internalize truth by painting it. Tell me how to paint the Christian faith.” The missionary opened his Bible to Luke 15 and said, “Paint the Parable of the Prodigal Son. If you can paint this, you will have the essence of the Christian faith.”
blocks.es_reference: Hace años, un misionero veterano en China se hizo amigo de un joven artista chino talentoso. A través de su amistad, el joven artista se hizo cristiano. Le dijo al misionero: «Yo mejor internalizo la verdad pintándola. Dígame cómo pintar la fe cristiana». El misionero abrió su Biblia en Lucas 15 y dijo: «Pinte la Parábola del Hijo Pródigo. Si puede pintar esto, tendrá la esencia de la fe cristiana».

blocks.en: The artist went to work. His first painting showed the Prodigal trudging down the road, head bowed, clothes ragged, shoulders slumped — the picture of remorse. So far, so good. But then he painted the Father. The Father was standing at the front gate. His arms were folded across his chest. His face was stern. He looked down the road at the returning son with an expression that said, I told you so.
blocks.es_reference: El artista se puso a trabajar. Su primer cuadro mostraba al Pródigo caminando penosamente por el camino, la cabeza inclinada, las ropas hechas jirones, los hombros caídos — el cuadro del remordimiento. Hasta ahí, bien. Pero luego pintó al Padre. El Padre estaba parado en la puerta del frente. Sus brazos estaban cruzados sobre el pecho. Su rostro estaba severo. Miraba al hijo que regresaba con una expresión que decía: te lo dije.

blocks.en: The missionary studied the painting and said gently, “Technically, this is beautiful. But you have missed the main message of the parable.” The artist asked, “How so?” The missionary answered, “The Father should not be standing at the gate with folded arms. The Father should be running. The whole parable turns on one thing — what God is like. He is anxious to love, quick to forgive, eager to reconcile. He runs.”
blocks.es_reference: El misionero estudió el cuadro y dijo amablemente: «Técnicamente, esto es hermoso. Pero ha perdido el mensaje principal de la parábola». El artista preguntó: «¿Cómo así?» El misionero respondió: «El Padre no debería estar parado en la puerta con los brazos cruzados. El Padre debería estar corriendo. La parábola entera gira sobre una sola cosa — cómo es Dios. Él está ansioso por amar, listo para perdonar, ávido por reconciliar. Él corre».

blocks.en: “But when he was still a great way off, his father saw him and had compassion, and ran and fell on his neck and kissed him.” (Luke 15:20, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: «Y cuando aún estaba lejos, su padre lo vio, y fue movido a misericordia, y corrió, y se echó sobre su cuello, y le besó.» (Lucas 15:20, RVG)

blocks.en: That conversation is our entire unit in miniature. A parable has one main point. Miss the main point and every detail you paint will sit slightly wrong on the canvas. Get the main point right and even the smallest detail will preach.
blocks.es_reference: Esa conversación es toda nuestra unidad en miniatura. Una parábola tiene un punto principal. Pierda el punto principal y cada detalle que pinte se sentará ligeramente mal en el lienzo. Acierte el punto principal y aun el detalle más pequeño predicará.

blocks.en: 2. What a Parable Is
blocks.es_reference: 2. Qué es una parábola

blocks.en: The Greek word parabolé literally means to throw alongside. Jesus would take a familiar earthly scene — a farmer sowing, a woman sweeping, a king holding a wedding feast — and throw it alongside a spiritual truth so the truth could be seen by familiar light. A parable is a short story drawn from ordinary life that carries one central spiritual lesson.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra griega parabolé significa literalmente arrojar al lado. Jesús tomaba una escena terrenal familiar — un labrador sembrando, una mujer barriendo, un rey haciendo un banquete de bodas — y la arrojaba al lado de una verdad espiritual para que la verdad pudiera verse a la luz familiar. Una parábola es una historia corta tomada de la vida cotidiana que carga una lección espiritual central.

blocks.en: Notice three things in that definition. Short story: the parable is a narrative, not a paragraph of doctrine. Ordinary life: the characters are farmers and shepherds and merchants and children, not angels and dragons. One central lesson: the parable is built around a principal point, not a code where every detail hides a separate doctrine. As this unit will show, context and Jesus's own explanations sometimes mean more than one detail carries real weight — but that weight always serves the parable's main thrust; it is never a license to mine each detail for a hidden meaning of its own.
blocks.es_reference: Note tres cosas en esa definición. Historia corta: la parábola es una narrativa, no un párrafo de doctrina. Vida cotidiana: los personajes son labradores, pastores, mercaderes, y niños, no ángeles ni dragones. Una lección central: la parábola está construida alrededor de un punto principal, no de un código donde cada detalle esconde una doctrina separada. Como mostrará esta unidad, el contexto y las propias explicaciones de Jesús a veces hacen que más de un detalle cargue peso real — pero ese peso siempre sirve al empuje principal de la parábola; nunca es una licencia para explotar cada detalle en busca de un significado oculto propio.

blocks.en: 3. The Difference Between Parable and Allegory
blocks.es_reference: 3. La diferencia entre parábola y alegoría

blocks.en: A parable makes one comparison. An allegory makes many. In an allegory, every detail stands for something else: this character is virtue, that character is vice, the road is life, the river is baptism, the trees are nations. Pilgrim’s Progress is an allegory; Bunyan tells us so. Christ’s parables are not.
blocks.es_reference: Una parábola hace una comparación. Una alegoría hace muchas. En una alegoría, cada detalle representa otra cosa: este personaje es la virtud, aquél es el vicio, el camino es la vida, el río es el bautismo, los árboles son naciones. El progreso del peregrino es una alegoría; Bunyan nos lo dice. Las parábolas de Cristo no lo son.

blocks.en: For more than a thousand years, faithful Christian teachers treated Jesus’ parables as allegories, with disastrous results. Augustine’s reading of the Good Samaritan is the classic case. He took every detail and assigned it a symbol. The traveler was Adam. Jerusalem was paradise. Jericho was the moon — standing for mortality. The robbers were Satan and his angels. The wounds were sin. The priest was the Mosaic law. The Levite was the Old Testament prophets. The Samaritan was Christ Himself. The donkey was Christ’s body. The inn was the church. The innkeeper was the apostle Paul. The two coins were the two testaments. The Samaritan’s promise to return was the Second Coming.
blocks.es_reference: Por más de mil años, maestros cristianos fieles trataron las parábolas de Jesús como alegorías, con resultados desastrosos. La lectura que hizo Agustín del Buen Samaritano es el caso clásico. Tomó cada detalle y le asignó un símbolo. El viajero era Adán. Jerusalén era el paraíso. Jericó era la luna — representando la mortalidad. Los ladrones eran Satanás y sus ángeles. Las heridas eran pecado. El sacerdote era la ley mosaica. El levita eran los profetas del Antiguo Testamento. El Samaritano era Cristo mismo. El asno era el cuerpo de Cristo. La posada era la iglesia. El posadero era el apóstol Pablo. Las dos monedas eran los dos testamentos. La promesa del Samaritano de regresar era la Segunda Venida.

blocks.en: Every detail symbolized something. The reading is ingenious. It is also wrong. Jesus told the parable in answer to a single question from a lawyer: And who is my neighbor? The whole parable answers one question: your neighbor is anyone who needs your mercy, no matter their race or religion. Augustine, by allegorizing, smothered Jesus’ central point under a pile of symbols. He stopped hearing what Jesus actually said.
blocks.es_reference: Cada detalle simbolizaba algo. La lectura es ingeniosa. También está equivocada. Jesús contó la parábola en respuesta a una sola pregunta de un intérprete de la ley: ¿y quién es mi prójimo? Toda la parábola responde una sola pregunta: su prójimo es cualquiera que necesite su misericordia, sin importar su raza ni su religión. Agustín, al alegorizar, sofocó el punto central de Jesús bajo una pila de símbolos. Dejó de oír lo que Jesús realmente dijo.

blocks.en: 4. Finding the Principal Point
blocks.es_reference: 4. Cómo hallar el punto principal

blocks.en: Here is the rule for every parable you ever preach. Find the one central point Jesus is making. Build your sermon on that point. Treat every other detail in the story as scenery — the furniture of the room, not the message of the room. The scenery is real. It is not random. But it is not symbolic, and the parable does not depend on it carrying secondary meanings.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí está la regla para cada parábola que predicará alguna vez. Encuentre el único punto central que Jesús está haciendo. Edifique su sermón sobre ese punto. Trate cada otro detalle de la historia como escenografía — los muebles del cuarto, no el mensaje del cuarto. La escenografía es real. No es al azar. Pero no es simbólica, y la parábola no depende de que cargue significados secundarios.

blocks.en: How do you find the central point? Three signals usually settle it. First, what question is Jesus answering? The Good Samaritan answers, Who is my neighbor? The Lost Sheep answers, Why is Jesus eating with sinners? The Vineyard Workers answers, Are the late-coming workers really equal to us? Second, who is in the audience? The Prodigal Son was told to grumbling Pharisees who resented the company Jesus kept — so the elder brother in the story is the audience caught in the mirror. Third, what is the climax of the parable? The line that the whole story is building toward usually carries the main point. In the Prodigal Son, the climax is the Father running. The whole parable is about that running.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Cómo encuentra el punto central? Tres señales generalmente lo resuelven. Primero, ¿qué pregunta está respondiendo Jesús? El Buen Samaritano responde: ¿quién es mi prójimo? La Oveja Perdida responde: ¿por qué come Jesús con pecadores? Los Obreros de la Viña responden: ¿son los obreros que llegan tarde realmente iguales a nosotros? Segundo, ¿quién está en la audiencia? El Hijo Pródigo fue contado a fariseos que murmuraban resentidos por la compañía que Jesús tenía — así que el hermano mayor en la historia es la audiencia atrapada en el espejo. Tercero, ¿cuál es el clímax de la parábola? La línea hacia la cual toda la historia está construyendo carga generalmente el punto principal. En el Hijo Pródigo, el clímax es el Padre que corre. Toda la parábola es acerca de esa carrera.

blocks.en: 5. The Artist’s Second Painting
blocks.es_reference: 5. El segundo cuadro del artista

blocks.en: The Chinese artist took the missionary’s correction and went back to his easel. He painted the parable again. The Prodigal looked the same — stooped, broken, walking home in shame. But this time the Father was different. The Father was running. His robes flapped in the wind. His face was full of joy and relief. And then the missionary noticed something strange. The Father’s shoes did not match. One shoe was red. The other was blue.
blocks.es_reference: El artista chino tomó la corrección del misionero y volvió a su caballete. Pintó la parábola otra vez. El Pródigo se veía igual — encorvado, quebrantado, caminando a casa avergonzado. Pero esta vez el Padre era diferente. El Padre estaba corriendo. Sus túnicas ondeaban en el viento. Su rostro estaba lleno de gozo y alivio. Y entonces el misionero notó algo extraño. Los zapatos del Padre no hacían juego. Un zapato era rojo. El otro era azul.

blocks.en: The missionary asked about the shoes. The artist explained, “The Father is so overjoyed to see his son coming home, so anxious to welcome him, that he grabs the two nearest shoes and runs out the door. It does not matter that they do not match. All that matters is that his son was lost and now is found.” That is what a parable rightly read looks like. One central point. The details serve the point.
blocks.es_reference: El misionero preguntó por los zapatos. El artista explicó: «El Padre está tan rebosante de gozo al ver a su hijo regresar, tan ansioso por recibirlo, que agarra los dos zapatos más cercanos y sale corriendo por la puerta. No importa que no hagan juego. Todo lo que importa es que su hijo se había perdido y ahora ha sido hallado». Así se ve una parábola leída correctamente. Un solo punto central. Los detalles sirven al punto.

blocks.en: 6. The Buddhist Prodigal — Same Plot, Opposite Point
blocks.es_reference: 6. El Pródigo budista: la misma trama, el punto opuesto

blocks.en: Buddhism has a parable that sounds almost the same as Jesus’. In the Lotus of Perfect Law, a son leaves his father’s house. He wastes years in misery. He returns in rags. But here the story takes a very different turn. The father recognizes the son; the son does not recognize the father. The father tells his servants to clean the son up — but does not reveal his identity. He gives the son humble work to do. He waits to see whether the son will become worthy. Only when the son has earned a better human nature, broken his old habits, and proven himself does the father finally reveal who he is and welcome the son as heir.
blocks.es_reference: El budismo tiene una parábola que suena casi igual a la de Jesús. En el Loto de la Ley Perfecta, un hijo deja la casa de su padre. Desperdicia años en miseria. Regresa en harapos. Pero aquí la historia toma un giro muy diferente. El padre reconoce al hijo; el hijo no reconoce al padre. El padre les dice a sus siervos que limpien al hijo — pero no revela su identidad. Le da al hijo un trabajo humilde que hacer. Espera a ver si el hijo se vuelve digno. Solo cuando el hijo ha ganado una mejor naturaleza humana, ha roto sus viejos hábitos, y se ha demostrado a sí mismo, el padre finalmente revela quién es y recibe al hijo como heredero.

blocks.en: Same plot. Opposite central point. The Buddhist parable teaches that the prodigal must earn his way back home, step by step, before grace can be offered. Jesus’ parable teaches the exact opposite. The Father runs while the son is still a great way off. The robe, the ring, and the shoes come before any confession the son has time to finish. Grace precedes earning. The whole story turns on it.
blocks.es_reference: La misma trama. El punto central opuesto. La parábola budista enseña que el pródigo debe ganarse el camino de regreso a casa, paso a paso, antes de que la gracia pueda ofrecerse. La parábola de Jesús enseña exactamente lo opuesto. El Padre corre mientras el hijo está aún lejos. La túnica, el anillo, y los zapatos vienen antes de cualquier confesión que el hijo tenga tiempo de terminar. La gracia precede al merecimiento. Toda la historia gira sobre esto.

blocks.en: Now here is the warning. A pastor who allegorizes Jesus’ parable — who turns every detail into a moral lesson the son must perform — will end up preaching the Buddhist version while quoting the Christian one. The plot looks the same. The point becomes the opposite. The cure for that is to lock down the one central point first, and let every detail serve it.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora aquí está la advertencia. Un pastor que alegorice la parábola de Jesús — que convierta cada detalle en una lección moral que el hijo deba cumplir — terminará predicando la versión budista mientras cita la cristiana. La trama se ve igual. El punto se vuelve lo opuesto. La cura para eso es fijar primero el único punto central, y dejar que cada detalle lo sirva.

blocks.en: 7. Three More Parables, One Central Point Each
blocks.es_reference: 7. Tres parábolas más, un punto central cada una

blocks.en: Try the rule on three other parables you will preach often.
blocks.es_reference: Pruebe la regla en otras tres parábolas que predicará a menudo.

blocks.en: The Sower (Mark 4). Four soils. Four results. One central point: the condition of the heart determines what happens when the Word is preached. Do not preach four separate sermons on four kinds of soil. Preach one sermon on whether the listener will receive the seed. The four soils are scenery serving that point.
blocks.es_reference: El Sembrador (Marcos 4). Cuatro suelos. Cuatro resultados. Un punto central: la condición del corazón determina lo que sucede cuando se predica la Palabra. No predique cuatro sermones separados sobre cuatro clases de suelo. Predique un solo sermón sobre si el oyente recibirá la semilla. Los cuatro suelos son escenografía que sirve a ese punto.

blocks.en: The Vineyard Workers (Matthew 20). Workers hired at different hours all paid the same wage at the end of the day. Do not preach this as a lesson in labor economics. It is not about fair wages. The central point is God’s generosity is not constrained by human bookkeeping. The parable comforts those who came to Christ late and rebukes those who think early arrival gives them a higher claim.
blocks.es_reference: Los Obreros de la Viña (Mateo 20). Obreros contratados a diferentes horas pagados todos con el mismo salario al final del día. No predique esto como una lección de economía laboral. No se trata de salarios justos. El punto central es la generosidad de Dios no está constreñida por la contabilidad humana. La parábola consuela a los que vinieron a Cristo tarde y reprende a los que piensan que su llegada temprana les da un reclamo mayor.

blocks.en: The Persistent Widow (Luke 18). A widow keeps coming back to an unjust judge until he grants her request. Do not allegorize the widow as the church and the judge as God. The point is not that God resembles an unjust judge. The point is the opposite: if even an unjust judge will yield to persistent pleading, how much more will a righteous God hear the persistent prayers of His own? The judge is scenery; persistence in prayer is the heart of the parable.
blocks.es_reference: La Viuda Persistente (Lucas 18). Una viuda sigue volviendo a un juez injusto hasta que él concede su petición. No alegorice la viuda como la iglesia y el juez como Dios. El punto no es que Dios se parezca a un juez injusto. El punto es lo opuesto: si aun un juez injusto cede a la súplica persistente, ¿cuánto más oirá un Dios justo las oraciones persistentes de los Suyos? El juez es escenografía; la persistencia en la oración es el corazón de la parábola.

blocks.en: 8. When Details Do Matter
blocks.es_reference: 8. Cuando los detalles sí importan

blocks.en: There is one exception to the rule, and it is an important one. When Jesus Himself explains a detail of a parable, that detail is no longer scenery — it is the Lord’s authorized symbol. In Mark 4 Jesus interprets the Sower for His disciples. He tells them the seed is the Word of God, the path is the hardened hearer, the rocky ground is the shallow hearer, the thorns are worldly cares, and the good soil is the receiving heart. Those interpretations are not the allegorizer’s invention; they are the Author’s authorized commentary. Use them.
blocks.es_reference: Hay una sola excepción a la regla, y es importante. Cuando Jesús mismo explica un detalle de una parábola, ese detalle ya no es escenografía — es el símbolo autorizado del Señor. En Marcos 4 Jesús interpreta al Sembrador para Sus discípulos. Les dice que la semilla es la Palabra de Dios, el camino es el oyente endurecido, el terreno pedregoso es el oyente superficial, los espinos son las preocupaciones del mundo, y la buena tierra es el corazón que recibe. Esas interpretaciones no son la invención del alegorista; son el comentario autorizado del Autor. Úselas.

blocks.en: When Jesus does not tell us what a detail represents, we do not get to decide for Him. The fatted calf in the Prodigal Son is not the Lord’s Supper, however cleverly it can be made to fit. The two coins in the Good Samaritan are not the two testaments. The widow’s judge is not the Father. Silence from the Author means scenery, not symbol.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Jesús no nos dice lo que un detalle representa, nosotros no podemos decidir por Él. El becerro engordado en el Hijo Pródigo no es la Cena del Señor, por más ingeniosamente que pueda hacérsele encajar. Las dos monedas en el Buen Samaritano no son los dos testamentos. El juez de la viuda no es el Padre. El silencio del Autor significa escenografía, no símbolo.

blocks.en: 9. Practical Method for Preaching a Parable
blocks.es_reference: 9. Método práctico para predicar una parábola

blocks.en: Five steps will keep your parable sermon honest. Read the parable in its setting — the question being asked, the audience being addressed, the chapter in which it sits. State the central point in one sentence — if you cannot write it on a single line, you have not yet found it. Test the central point against the climax of the story — the most emotional or surprising line in the parable usually carries the weight. Build the sermon on that central point — not on every detail in turn. Use the details as illustration, not as separate doctrines.
blocks.es_reference: Cinco pasos mantendrán honesto su sermón parabólico. Lea la parábola en su entorno — la pregunta que se hace, la audiencia a la que se dirige, el capítulo en el cual se ubica. Declare el punto central en una sola oración — si no puede escribirlo en una sola línea, todavía no lo ha encontrado. Pruebe el punto central contra el clímax de la historia — la línea más emotiva o sorprendente de la parábola generalmente carga el peso. Edifique el sermón sobre ese punto central — no sobre cada detalle uno a uno. Use los detalles como ilustración, no como doctrinas separadas.

blocks.en: A parable preached this way will burn through your congregation the way Jesus meant it to. A parable allegorized will impress them with your cleverness for ten minutes and feed them nothing for the week. Choose the burning one.
blocks.es_reference: Una parábola predicada de esta manera arderá en su congregación como Jesús quiso. Una parábola alegorizada los impresionará con su ingenio por diez minutos y no los alimentará nada para la semana. Escoja la que arde.

blocks.en: 10. Paint the Father Running
blocks.es_reference: 10. Pinte al Padre corriendo

blocks.en: Henri Nouwen once spent two hours in the Hermitage in St. Petersburg standing before Rembrandt’s painting of the Prodigal Son. As the daylight outside shifted, the painting shifted with it — different details rising into the light at different angles of the sun. Nouwen wrote, There were as many paintings in the Prodigal Son as there were changes in the day.
blocks.es_reference: Henri Nouwen una vez pasó dos horas en el Hermitage en San Petersburgo parado ante el cuadro de Rembrandt del Hijo Pródigo. Mientras la luz del día afuera cambiaba, el cuadro cambiaba con ella — diferentes detalles surgiendo a la luz en diferentes ángulos del sol. Nouwen escribió: había tantos cuadros en el Hijo Pródigo como había cambios en el día.

blocks.en: A great parable is like that. It has many facets. Many details. Many angles from which to admire it. But it has only one central light source. Find that source and every detail glows where it sits. Lose that source and the painting goes dark.
blocks.es_reference: Una gran parábola es así. Tiene muchas facetas. Muchos detalles. Muchos ángulos desde los cuales admirarla. Pero tiene una sola fuente central de luz. Encuentre esa fuente y cada detalle brilla donde está. Pierda esa fuente y el cuadro se oscurece.

blocks.en: Pastor, when you preach a parable, paint the Father running. Paint the question being answered. Paint the single light Jesus shone into the room. The mismatched shoes will take care of themselves.
blocks.es_reference: Pastor, cuando predique una parábola, pinte al Padre corriendo. Pinte la pregunta que se está respondiendo. Pinte la luz única que Jesús hizo brillar en el cuarto. Los zapatos desiguales se cuidarán solos.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, the Chinese artist's first painting of the Prodigal Son was wrong because:
options: The colors were too dark
The Prodigal looked too healthy
The Father was painted standing with folded arms instead of running
The artist had never read the parable
mc.why: Correct. The whole parable turns on what God is like — anxious to love, quick to forgive, eager to reconcile. The Father RUNS while the son is still a great way off. A stern Father with folded arms misses the parable's central point.

mc.stem: The Greek word "parabolé" literally means:
options: To hide a truth
To prove a doctrine
To throw alongside
To memorize
mc.why: Correct. Jesus would take a familiar earthly scene — a farmer, a woman sweeping, a king — and throw it alongside a spiritual truth so the truth could be seen by familiar light. That is what a parable does: it places one thing next to another.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, the difference between a parable and an allegory is:
options: Parables are in the Old Testament, allegories in the New
A parable makes one comparison; an allegory makes many
Parables are spoken, allegories are written
There is no real difference between them
mc.why: Correct. An allegory assigns symbolic meaning to every detail — Pilgrim's Progress is an allegory. Jesus' parables make ONE central comparison, with the details as scenery. Treating a parable as an allegory smothers Christ's central point.

mc.stem: Augustine's allegorical reading of the Good Samaritan (the inn = the church, the two coins = the two testaments, etc.) is used in this lesson as:
options: The classic case of how allegorizing smothers a parable's central point
A model of careful exegesis
A reading the modern church should recover
An exception that proves the rule
mc.why: Correct. Augustine assigned a symbol to every detail. Ingenious, but he stopped hearing what Jesus actually said. Jesus told the parable to answer one question — "Who is my neighbor?" — and the answer was buried under a pile of symbols.

mc.stem: The single question Jesus was answering in the Parable of the Good Samaritan was:
options: "What does it cost to follow me?"
"Why does God allow evil?"
"Should we travel from Jerusalem to Jericho?"
"Who is my neighbor?"
mc.why: Correct. A lawyer asked, "Who is my neighbor?" The whole parable answers that one question: your neighbor is anyone who needs your mercy, no matter their race or religion. The audience question is the first key to the central point.

mc.stem: The lesson names three signals that usually help the pastor identify a parable's central point. The first is:
options: What question is Jesus answering?
Which Greek word is repeated?
How many verses does the parable take?
Which Old Testament prophet is referenced?
mc.why: Correct. The Good Samaritan answers "Who is my neighbor?" The Lost Sheep answers "Why is Jesus eating with sinners?" The Vineyard Workers answers "Are the latecomers really equal?" Find the question, and you have found the central point.

mc.stem: The second signal for finding a parable's central point is:
options: The translator's footnote
The chapter heading in your study Bible
The denomination you belong to
The audience originally hearing the parable
mc.why: Correct. The Prodigal Son was told to grumbling Pharisees who resented Jesus' company with sinners. That is why the parable's elder brother features so prominently — the audience is caught in the mirror. Know the audience and you find the point.

mc.stem: The third signal for finding a parable's central point is:
options: The length of the parable
The climax — the most emotional or surprising line in the story
The geography mentioned
The cost of materials in the story
mc.why: Correct. The climax usually carries the main point. In the Prodigal Son, the climax is the Father running. The whole parable is about that running — every other detail serves it. Find the climax, you find the heart.

mc.stem: The Father in the Prodigal Son painting wears mismatched shoes (one red, one blue) because:
options: Persian fashion of the day required it
The artist could not afford matching paint
The shoes represent the two testaments
He grabbed the two nearest shoes in his hurry to run out and welcome his son
mc.why: Correct. The artist made the Father so overjoyed and eager that he grabbed whatever shoes were closest and ran. The shoes are not a symbol of a doctrine; they are an image of the haste of grace. Notice — this is scenery serving the central point.

mc.stem: The Buddhist parable of the prodigal son (from the Lotus of Perfect Law) differs from Jesus' parable in that:
options: The Buddhist son never returns home
The Buddhist father reveals his identity immediately
The Buddhist father waits until the son becomes worthy step by step before welcoming him
The Buddhist parable does not feature a father
mc.why: Correct. Same plot, opposite point. The Buddhist parable teaches that the son must EARN his way back. Jesus' parable teaches the OPPOSITE — the Father runs while the son is still a great way off. Grace precedes earning. A pastor who allegorizes Jesus' parable can end up preaching the Buddhist version.

mc.stem: The central point of the Parable of the Sower (Mark 4) is:
options: The condition of the heart determines what happens when the Word is preached
Farmers should sow seed more carefully
There are exactly four types of human beings
Birds, rocks, thorns, and good ground all symbolize one thing
mc.why: Correct. Do not preach four separate sermons on four kinds of soil. Preach one sermon on whether the listener will receive the seed. The four soils are scenery serving that single point — and the point is the responding heart.

mc.stem: The central point of the Parable of the Vineyard Workers (Matthew 20) is:
options: A lesson in fair labor wages
God's generosity is not constrained by human bookkeeping
Latecomers should be paid less for less work
The vineyard owner was secretly unjust
mc.why: Correct. The parable comforts those who came to Christ late and rebukes those who think early arrival gives them a higher claim. It is not about wages or unfairness — it is about a generosity that exceeds bookkeeping.

mc.stem: The central point of the Parable of the Persistent Widow (Luke 18) is:
options: God resembles an unjust judge
Widows should always pursue lawsuits
If even an unjust judge yields to persistent pleading, how much more will a righteous God hear His own?
The judge represents the Roman Empire
mc.why: Correct. The parable argues from contrast, not from similarity. God is NOT like the unjust judge; God is the opposite. The point is to encourage persistence in prayer to a Father who is not reluctant but eager to hear.

mc.stem: The one exception to the rule "parables are not allegories" is:
options: When the parable is more than ten verses long
When the parable involves animals
When Jesus Himself explains a detail of the parable
When the parable appears in more than one Gospel
mc.why: Correct. When Jesus interprets the Sower for His disciples — the seed is the Word, the path is the hardened hearer, the rocky ground is the shallow hearer — those are not the allegorizer's invention. They are the Author's authorized commentary. Use them.

mc.stem: The lesson summarizes: when Jesus does not tell us what a detail represents:
options: Silence from the Author means scenery, not symbol
We get to decide for Him
The pastor should pick the most spiritual meaning
Tradition fills in what Christ omitted
mc.why: Correct. The fatted calf is not the Lord's Supper. The two coins are not the two testaments. The widow's judge is not the Father. When the Author is silent on what a detail means, the detail is SCENERY — not a symbol waiting for human invention.

mc.stem: The lesson recommends five practical steps for preaching a parable. The first step is:
options: Pick a memorable illustration
Read the parable in its setting — the question, the audience, the chapter
Choose a contemporary application
Decide on a memorable title
mc.why: Correct. Read the parable in its setting first: what question is being asked, what audience is being addressed, what chapter it sits inside. Setting is the source of the central point. Skip this step and the rest of the sermon drifts.

mc.stem: The second practical step the lesson recommends is:
options: Memorize the parable in Greek
State the central point in one sentence
Find five commentaries that agree with each other
Look up the Hebrew word for parable
mc.why: Correct. If you cannot write the central point on a single line, you have not yet found it. Forcing one-sentence clarity is a discipline that exposes muddy thinking and prevents allegorical drift.

mc.stem: The Henri Nouwen / Rembrandt Hermitage story (two hours in front of the Prodigal Son painting) illustrates:
options: The importance of expensive art for spiritual life
The danger of museum visits
The fact that all great Russian painters were Christians
A great parable has many facets and angles — but one central light source
mc.why: Correct. Nouwen wrote, "There were as many paintings in the Prodigal Son as there were changes in the day." A parable is like that: many facets, many details, many angles — but one central light source. Find that source and every detail glows.

mc.stem: According to this lesson, what does an allegorized sermon do to the listening congregation?
options: Impresses them with the pastor's cleverness for ten minutes and feeds them nothing for the week
Always converts the lost
Provides the deepest possible insight into Scripture
Helps everyone memorize the Bible faster
mc.why: Correct. Allegorized sermons can be ingenious. They cannot feed the soul, because they substitute the pastor's invention for Christ's words. Ten minutes of admiration, then a week of nothing. A parable rightly preached burns for the whole week.

mc.stem: The closing charge of this unit to the pastor is:
options: Avoid all parables in preaching
Allegorize freely whenever possible
Memorize every parable in Greek
Paint the Father running — preach the single central light Jesus shone into the room, and the details will take care of themselves
mc.why: Correct. Paint the Father running. Paint the question being answered. Paint the single light Jesus shone into the room. The mismatched shoes — every supporting detail of the story — will take care of themselves.

fill.prompt: "But when he was still a great way off, his father saw him and had compassion, and ____ and fell on his neck and kissed him." (Luke 15:20)
The Greek word ____, from which we get "parable," literally means to throw alongside.
A parable makes one comparison; the kind of story in which every detail stands for something else is called ____.
The classic case of allegorizing a parable is the reading of the Good Samaritan by ____, in which Jericho was the moon and the innkeeper was the apostle Paul.
Jesus told the Good Samaritan to answer a lawyer's single question: "And who is my ____?"
Find the one central point of a parable and treat every other detail as ____, the furniture of the room, not the message of the room.
Unlike the Buddhist story, in which the returning son must first prove himself before his father welcomes him, Jesus' parable of the Prodigal Son teaches that grace precedes ____.
The central point of the parable of the Sower is that the condition of the ____ determines what happens when the Word is preached.
In the parable of the Vineyard Workers, the central point is that God's ____ is not constrained by human bookkeeping.
In the parable of the Persistent Widow, the unjust judge is scenery; the main point is persistence in ____.

sa.prompt: Tell the story of the Chinese artist and the missionary's correction of his first painting of the Prodigal Son. Explain what it teaches about reading parables.
sa.model: A missionary told a Chinese artist who wanted to paint the Christian faith to paint the Parable of the Prodigal Son. When the artist got it right, the central figure was the Father running to meet his son, robes flapping, full of joy. The story teaches that a parable has one central point — here, the running, welcoming Father — not a dozen scattered symbols to paint.

sa.prompt: Define a parable in your own words and contrast it with an allegory. Why does this distinction matter for the pastor?
sa.model: Most parables make a single central comparison, with the rest of the story serving as scenery that carries that one point — though a few, like the Wheat and Tares, come with several correspondences Jesus Himself supplies (Matthew 13:36-43). An allegory, by contrast, assigns the interpreter's own separate meaning to every detail without textual warrant. The distinction matters because if the pastor allegorizes Jesus' parables on his own authority, he will find a dozen hidden meanings Jesus never intended and miss the point or points He did intend.

sa.prompt: Describe Augustine's allegorical reading of the Good Samaritan and explain why this lesson treats it as a cautionary example.
sa.model: Augustine read the Good Samaritan as an allegory, assigning a symbol to every detail — the inn became the church, the innkeeper Paul, the two coins the two testaments, the Samaritan Christ. The lesson treats this as a cautionary example because once each detail is a symbol, the interpreter, not Jesus, controls the meaning, and the parable's real point is buried.

sa.prompt: The lesson names three signals that help identify a parable's central point. Name and briefly explain each signal.
sa.model: Three signals help find a parable's central point. First, the question or situation that prompted the parable. Second, the audience Jesus was addressing. Third, the climax of the story, where the weight falls. Reading these signals together keeps the interpreter on the one central point rather than wandering into the scenery.

sa.prompt: Tell the Buddhist Prodigal Son story (from the Lotus of Perfect Law) and explain how it has the same plot as Jesus' parable but the opposite central point.
sa.model: The Buddhist Prodigal in the Lotus Sutra has the same plot as Jesus' parable but the opposite central point: the son must work for years to earn his way and prove himself worthy before the father will receive him. In Jesus' parable the Father runs out first — grace precedes the son's worthiness. Same story, opposite gospel.

sa.prompt: State in one sentence the central point of the Parable of the Sower (Mark 4), and explain why the four soils are scenery rather than four separate doctrines.
sa.model: The central point of the Parable of the Sower is that the same seed — the Word of God — meets different hearts and only the receptive heart bears fruit. The four soils are scenery serving that one point, not four separate doctrines to be mined individually. Read as four doctrines, the parable loses its single message about how the heart receives the Word.

sa.prompt: State the central point of the Parable of the Vineyard Workers (Matthew 20) and explain why this parable is NOT about labor economics.
sa.model: The central point of the Vineyard Workers is the owner's generosity, not labor economics. He pays the same wage to those hired late as to those hired early, and when they grumble he answers that he may do as he wishes with his own. The parable is about grace — God's equal, undeserved generosity — not a lesson in fair wages.

sa.prompt: State the central point of the Parable of the Persistent Widow (Luke 18) and explain why the judge is a CONTRAST to God, not a symbol of God.
sa.model: The central point of the Persistent Widow is that we should always pray and not lose heart. The unjust judge is a contrast to God, not a symbol of Him: if even a corrupt judge will finally answer a persistent widow, how much more will the righteous God answer His own. Reading the judge as a symbol of the Father reverses the parable's meaning.

sa.prompt: Explain the one exception to the rule "parables are not allegories" and why this exception is limited to that single case.
sa.model: The one exception to 'parables are not allegories' is when Jesus Himself explains the details, as He does with the Parable of the Sower — there the seed, the birds, and the soils each get a meaning straight from His mouth. That is authorized commentary. Where Jesus does not assign a meaning, the interpreter does not get to decide one; the exception is limited to His own explanations.

sa.prompt: List the five practical steps the lesson recommends for preaching a parable and briefly describe each.
sa.model: Five steps guide preaching a parable: first establish its setting and the question that prompted it; second state the one central point in a single sentence; third test every detail against that point, refusing to allegorize what Jesus left as scenery; fourth build the sermon toward the parable's climax; and fifth preach that one point home. Setting, sentence, test, climax, point.
